input:
In order to understand phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point, it is necessary to appreciate what the equilibrium condition means. A pure component at its boiling point maintains liquid and vapour in phase equilibrium when the chemical potential of the component is equal in the two phases. The chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of the driving force for a species to leave a phase; when the two values are equal, neither phase gains the component at the expense of the other, and transfer across the interface continues in both directions at equal rates. This condition is stated here in words because it serves as the definition that the rest of the discussion relies upon: boiling is essentially the visible sign of the equality, rather than its underlying cause.

Furthermore, at the boiling point, the temperature and the pressure of the pure component are not independent variables. Fixing the pressure fixes the boiling temperature, because the equality of chemical potential can only be satisfied at one temperature for that pressure. Increasing the pressure increases the temperature at which the two chemical potentials meet, which helps to explain why a change in pressure shifts the boiling point instead of breaking the equilibrium. Additionally, the vapour formed has the same composition as the liquid, since the component is pure; nothing in the condition acts to separate one part of the substance from another.

The equality also determines what any disturbance will do. Heat added at the boiling point converts liquid into vapour at constant temperature, and the chemical potentials remain equal while both phases are present. Only when one phase has disappeared can the temperature begin to move again. The quantitative form of the pressure dependence is provided by the Clapeyron equation, which relates the slope of the boiling curve to the enthalpy of vaporisation and the volume change on boiling. Importantly, this equation is a direct consequence of the equality described above, and it introduces no second condition.
